full_judgment:
5. The learned Advocate for the applicant-petitioner (insurance company) strenuously argues that the insurer of the cargo may not have the competence to file the admiralty suit as a plaintiff by invoking jurisdiction under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 for loss or damage to the cargo carried by the said vessel, but it can certainly be added as a co-plaintiff in view of Rule 12 of the Admiralty Rules as it has acquired interest in the said vessel during the pendency of the suit after having been subrogated to the rights and remedies of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate for defendants, on the other hand, submits in reply that since the applicant-petitioner has no right to invoke admiralty jurisdiction as plaintiff under section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 it cannot for the same reason be allowed to be added as co-plaintiff in the present suit. 

 6. The learned Advocate while opposing the prayer for addition of the applicant-petitioner as a co-plaintiff in the suit referred to the cases of Sadharan Bima Corporation vs Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and others reported in 43 DLR 322, Eastern Insurance Company vs DB Deviz Nakliyati TAB and others reported in 46 DLR (AD) 185 and another unreported decision in the case of Md Yunus vs Barbar Wilhelinsin Agencies Pte Ltd and others. 

 8. Keeping this background in mind it will be advisable to consider section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 and Rule 12 of the Admiralty Rules which came into operation on the 1st July, 1912. It appears from the language employed in section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 that the owner or assignee or consignee of the bill of lading of any goods arrived in Bangladesh may claim for damages/ compensation by filing admiralty suit if the damage to the goods is caused by negligence, misconduct, breach of duty or breach of contract committed by the owner, master or crew of the ship. The applicant-petitioner is an insurer of the cargo and not the owner, consignee or assignee of the bill of lading thereof and, as such, it cannot bring any action for the said loss of the cargo in question in admiralty jurisdiction in Bangladesh. 

 9. In the case of Sadharan Bima Corporation vs Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and others reported in 43 DLR 322, Sadharan Bima Corporation instituted admiralty suit against the offending vessel for compensation on account of damage and loss to the cargo carried by the said ship. Defendant No. 1 namely, the vessel in question in that suit, challenged the locus standi of the plaintiff for bringing the Admiralty action by filling an application under Order 7 rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for return of the plaint. The Admiralty Court in the High Court Division by the aforesaid judgment returned the plaint holding that the plaintiff as insurer of the cargo had no locus standi in terms of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. 

 10. In the case of Eastern Insurance Co. Ltd vs DB Deviz Nakliati TAB and others vide 46 DLR (AD) 185 at the leave granting stage it was held that the insurer was neither an owner, nor a consignee or assignee of the bill of lading in respect of the goods concerned and, as such, had no locus standi to file the suit in Admiralty Court in view of section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1816. 

 14. The important question that is raised by the application under consideration is, whether an insurer of the cargo carried by the vessel in question can be added as a co-plaintiff in an admiralty suit on the strength of subrogation. There is no dispute and it is a settled position of law that an insurer does not acquire any independent right to invoke admiralty jurisdiction within the meaning of section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 as it is neither an owner nor a consignee or assignee of the bill of lading of the cargo. 

 16. Moreover, whether a third person can be added in a pending admiralty suit, a different consideration of law is to be resorted to Proceedings before the Admiralty Court is a civil proceeding as it involves the assertion of enforcement of a civil right. Rules 3 and 51 of the Admiralty Rules, if read with sections 117 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, will show that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to the proceedings before the Admiralty Court unless it is excluded by any rule. There appears to be no rule making the provision of Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure inapplicable to the original civil jurisdiction of the High Court Division, namely, its admiralty jurisdiction. The case of Saleh Steel Industries Ltd vs TSS ''Pacific Abeto'' and others vide 35 DLR (AD) (1983) 188 and Khaian Bittahin Co-operative Society Ltd vs Nagendra Mahsya Das vide 45 DLR 502 may be profitably referred to in this connection. Order 1 rule 10(2) permits addition of a third party as a co-plaintiff, keeping in view the nature of its claim, if its presence is necessary in order to dispose of the suit completely and for adjudication of all the questions involved in the suit between the parties in order to avoid multiplicity of proceedings and conflict of decision. Questions involved in the suit means not merely the questions involved in the suit as originally framed. Similarly, the Court has power to add not only those persons who were necessary parties on the date of the suit but also persons who subsequently become necessary parties. Keeping these considerations in view I have no hesitation to hold that the applicant-petitioner is entitled to be added as a co-plaintiff. 

 17. This apart, if the applicant-petitioner is forced to file another suit in the ordinary civil Court his action is likely to be prejudiced for the non-availability of the material documents to prove the liability of the offending vessel. An insurer of the cargo has no independent right to invoke admiralty jurisdiction as a plaintiff in view of section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861, but it can be added as a co-plaintiff in a pending admiralty suit provided it acquires interest in the vessel on the basis of letter of subrogation. In this view of the matter and in the facts and circumstances of the present case, I find merit in the application of the applicant-petitioner for being added as a co-plaintiff.
